Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
always plan an escape route before entering a place

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

vignette: When Minh was twenty-two, a routine trade delegation in his homeland turned into confinement. The men who escorted him out of the meeting room never explained the shift in their demeanor, only the heavy click of the door locking behind them. For weeks, he slept on a thin mat in a windowless concrete cell, surrounded by guards who paced the floorboards and communicated in low, deliberate tones. The space was tight, forcing him to keep his eyes lowered, his neck permanently arched against the strain of looking up at the barred ventilation grate. In that small room, he stepped outside his own mind. He watched himself as if from the corner, detaching himself from the memories of the hunger and the waiting, until the days blurred into a single continuous loop. He came to avoid the calendar date of his arrest, marking it in silence, pretending the year had skipped entirely. Decades later, the memories do not arrive as stories he can tell. They arrive as a film that plays over and over, frame by frame: the scrape of boots on concrete, the weight of a guard’s hand on his shoulder, the dull ache in his neck. When his wife, Clara, asks him to talk about it, he knows what happened. He can feel the memory in his ribs, but when he opens his mouth, the words scatter. He loses the thread halfway through a sentence, his fingers tightening around his teacup, certain that trying to piece it together will only unravel him. He stops trying, though the knowledge of what occurred sits heavy and unspoken. The world outside the cell never felt safe again. Sudden movements now catch him in the chest—a mechanic dropping a wrench at a client’s garage, a delivery driver stepping quickly onto his driveway. His body responds before his mind can catch up: his stomach turns to water, nausea rising like tide, and his neck muscles lock into a familiar, grinding tension. He finds himself scanning every room before stepping through the doorway, mapping the exits, counting the doors, always leaving a clear path to the street. Even inside his own home, he feels on guard. He sits with his back to the wall during dinners, aware of the quiet hum of the refrigerator, the creak of the floorboards, maintaining a steady vigil that never quite drops. Plumbing work, once a steady trade, now demands constant calculation. At sixty-nine, Minh still climbs into crawl spaces and basements, but he no longer enters unfamiliar homes without first noting the location of every stairwell and window. He works primarily with men, and when a client or a fellow tradesman stands alone with him in a tight laundry room, the air grows heavy. He keeps his movements deliberate, his gaze fixed on the pipes, aware of how easily a sudden gesture could trigger that old, familiar nausea. He has come to believe that scanning the room is simply part of the job, a necessary step before picking up his tool belt. The visit to the clinic began on a Tuesday afternoon, after a job site where a new apprentice lunged forward to hand him a wrench, and Minh had dropped his gear, his vision swimming, his neck seizing until he had to sit on a stacked pile of drywall until the wave passed. Clara noticed the way he flinched at car doors slamming, the way he avoided the grocery store aisle where a man had once shouted at him, the way the calendar date of his detention now brought a cold sweat even at his age. She urged him to seek help, not for the work, but for the quiet life he once promised her. He sits in the waiting room now, one hand resting lightly on his neck, hoping the conversation will not unravel the careful distance he has kept for decades, yet dreading the possibility that he will finally have to face the film playing in his head without the tools he has used to keep it at bay.
